title: Scalar quantity
body: A scalar is a quantity described by magnitude only.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.1 "Scalars are quantities described by magnitude only"

title: Vector quantity
body: A vector is a quantity described by both magnitude and direction.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.1 "vectors are quantities described by both magnitude and direction"

title: Scalar vs. vector examples
body: The CED's examples of scalar and vector quantities in kinematics.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.3 "Distance and speed are examples of scalar quantities, while position, displacement, velocity, and acceleration are examples of vector quantities"

title: Vector arrow representation
body: A vector is drawn as an arrow whose direction is the vector's direction and whose length is proportional to its magnitude.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.2 "Vectors can be visually modeled as arrows with appropriate direction and lengths proportional to their magnitude"

title: Unit vector notation
body: \vec{r} = A\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + C\hat{k}
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.4.i "sum of their constituent components in the x-, y-, and z-directions, denoted by i, j, and k"

title: Position vector and its unit vector
body: The position vector of a point is denoted \vec{r}, and the unit vector in the direction of the position vector is denoted \hat{r}.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.4.ii "The position vector of a point is given by r"

title: Resultant vector (sum of components)
body: \vec{C} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} = (A_x + B_x)\hat{i} + (A_y + B_y)\hat{j}
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.4.iii "A resultant vector is the vector sum of the addend vectors' components"

title: Signs in one dimension
body: In a given one-dimensional coordinate system, opposite directions are denoted by opposite signs.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.5 "opposite directions are denoted by opposite signs"

title: Object model
body: In the object model the size, shape, and internal configuration are ignored, and the object may be treated as a single point with extensive properties such as mass and charge.
ced_evidence: 1.2.A.1 "the size, shape, and internal configuration are ignored"

title: Displacement
body: \Delta x = x - x_0
ced_evidence: 1.2.A.2 "Displacement is the change in an object's position"

title: Average velocity
body: \vec{v}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{x}}{\Delta t}
ced_evidence: 1.2.B.2 "Average velocity is the displacement of an object divided by the interval of time"

title: Average acceleration
body: \vec{a}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}
ced_evidence: 1.2.B.3 "Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the interval of time"

title: When an object is accelerating
body: An object is accelerating if the magnitude and/or the direction of its velocity is changing.
caution: Acceleration is not only speeding up or negative values; slowing down and changing direction also count, and the sign depends on the chosen axis.
ced_evidence: 1.2.B.4 "accelerating if either the magnitude and/or direction of the object's velocity are changing"

title: Instantaneous value
body: As the time interval used to calculate an average value of a quantity approaches zero, the average approaches the value of the quantity at that instant, called the instantaneous value.
ced_evidence: 1.2.C.1 "the average value of that quantity approaches the value of the quantity at that instant"

title: Instantaneous velocity
body: \vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}, \qquad v_x = \frac{dx}{dt}
ced_evidence: 1.2.C.1.i "derivative of position with respect to time"

title: Instantaneous acceleration
body: \vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}, \qquad a_x = \frac{dv_x}{dt}
ced_evidence: 1.2.C.1.ii "derivative of velocity with respect to time"

title: Moving between x(t), v(t), and a(t)
body: Time-dependent position, velocity, and acceleration functions are related by differentiation (position to velocity to acceleration) and integration (the reverse).
ced_evidence: 1.2.C.2 "can be determined using differentiation and integration"

title: Representations of motion
body: The CED's five ways to represent motion.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.1 "motion diagrams, figures, graphs, equations, and narrative descriptions"

title: Constant acceleration: velocity-time equation
body: v_x = v_{x0} + a_x t
caution: Valid only for constant acceleration; written for x but usable in any single dimension.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.2 "v x = v x0 + ax t"

title: Constant acceleration: position-time equation
body: x = x_0 + v_{x0} t + \tfrac{1}{2} a_x t^2
caution: Valid only for constant acceleration; written for x but usable in any single dimension.

title: Constant acceleration: velocity-position equation
caution: Valid only for constant acceleration; written for x but usable in any single dimension.

title: Gravitational acceleration near Earth
body: Near Earth's surface the vertical acceleration due to gravity is downward and constant, with g \approx 10 m/s^2 used for numerical work.
caution: The 10 m/s^2 value is the expected one, but correctly using 9.8 or 9.81 m/s^2 is not penalized.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.3 "downward, constant"; Boundary Statement "g ≈ 10 m/s^2 will be used"

title: Reading x(t), v(t), a(t) graphs
body: Relationships among position, velocity, and acceleration graphs as functions of time.

items.label: Slope of tangent on x–t graph
Slope of tangent on v–t graph
Area under a–t curve
items.meaning: Change in velocity during the interval

ced_evidence: 1.3.A.4 "Graphs of position, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time can be used to find the relationships between those quantities"

title: Displacement from area under v–t graph
body: \Delta x = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v_x(t)\,dt
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.4.iii "displacement of an object during a time interval is equal to the area under the curve"

title: Change in velocity from area under a–t graph
body: \Delta v_x = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} a_x(t)\,dt
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.4.iv "change in velocity of an object during a time interval is equal to the area under the curve"

title: Reference frame determines measurements
body: The choice of reference frame determines the direction and magnitude of quantities measured by an observer in that frame.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.1 "The choice of reference frame will determine the direction and magnitude of quantities"

title: Relative velocity by vector addition
body: The observed velocity of an object combines the object's velocity and the velocity of the observer's reference frame, using vector addition or subtraction to convert between frames.
ced_evidence: 1.4.B.2 / 1.4.B.2.i "involves the addition or subtraction of vectors"

title: Acceleration is the same in all inertial frames
body: The acceleration of any object is the same as measured from all inertial reference frames.
ced_evidence: 1.4.B.2.ii "The acceleration of any object is the same as measured from all inertial reference frames"

title: Default frame assumption
body: Unless otherwise stated, the frame of reference of any problem may be assumed to be inertial.
ced_evidence: Boundary Statement "Unless otherwise stated, the frame of reference of any problem may be assumed to be inertial"

title: Analyze 2D motion by components
body: Motion in two dimensions is analyzed with one-dimensional kinematic relationships applied to each component separately, and motion in one dimension can change without changing a perpendicular dimension.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.1 "analyzed using one-dimensional kinematic relationships if the motion is separated into components"; 1.5.A.3

title: Components may differ and be nonuniform
body: Velocity and acceleration may be different in each dimension and may be nonuniform.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.2 "Velocity and acceleration may be different in each dimension and may be nonuniform"

title: Projectile motion
body: Projectile motion is a special case of two-dimensional motion with zero acceleration in one dimension and constant, nonzero acceleration in the second dimension.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.4 "zero acceleration in one dimension and constant, nonzero acceleration in the second dimension"
